paragraphs.text: Both the divine Scripture has handed down, and the word of our teaching has quietly shown to those eager to learn, that man was made in the image and likeness of God. The diligent among you who listen will certainly remember how we completed our discussion of these matters: being "in the image" refers first of all to man's lordship and his rule over all things, while the "likeness" of this image is taken to mean the perfecting of the virtues. Now, brothers, we must show and set out clearly how man, who was honoured more highly than all God's works, fell from the honoured, original beauty of the divine stamp into the nature and likeness of the irrational beasts. For though he was the image of God, the lover of mankind, he darkened himself with his vices and dulled himself with his transgressions, and truly he was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them. How man became like the senseless cattle we must see from his deeds themselves, not so that we may find fault with what is past, but so that we may set right what is present. For the story of Adam and the whole history of those who came before are read, not so that we may praise or blame those who came before, but so that we may imitate virtue and turn away from vice. "These things," says the wonderful Paul, "were written for our instruction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come." So the first man cast away, through his disobedience, the image made in the likeness of God, made it something for demons to trample on, and disgraced it with the likenesses of irrational beasts. One man, because of the savagery and tyranny of his ways, he turned into a lion rather than a man; another he made a wolf because of his greed for plunder. And Scripture bears witness, saying: "Your rulers are like roaring lions, and your judges like the wolves of Arabia," calling the savage and tyrannical lions, and those who plunder and have their eyes on gain wolves. Do you see how man, made in the image of God, was brought down to the rank of the irrational beasts? When a man plays the tyrant, he is called a lion; when he plunders, he receives the name of wolf; and when he wallows in unbridled desires and, like the beasts, is carried away into lawless deeds, man is found to be a horse in turn. For it says: "They became stallions mad for females; each one neighed after his neighbour's wife." Others again vice has turned from men into dogs. Dogs—why? Because of their barking, because they always delight in uproar and turmoil. Of these the blessed David, too, cries out through prophecy in the person of the Saviour: "Dogs have surrounded me." And who are the dogs? "A gang of evildoers has encircled me." Others again Scripture calls swine: those who wallow in the pit of outrageous deeds. Of these the Lord says through the evangelist: "Do not throw what is holy to the dogs, or your pearls before swine." Do you see how many forms man takes, and how that image made in the likeness of God was brought down to the likeness of the irrational beasts—not because anyone else forced him, but because man cast himself down? For Scripture did not ascribe the transgression to necessity but to the free choice of one who was honoured and did not recognize his honour. For it says: "Man, being in honour, did not understand." Come now, if you will, let us consider again how Scripture calls certain others foxes, because their way of thinking professes to be one thing while being shifty, cunning and full of hypocrisy. That is why the Saviour calls Herod a fox: he was shifty in his opinions and cunning in his thoughts, living in ungodliness while putting on the appearance of godliness. For when some people came and told him, "Herod wants to see you," that holy and mighty voice answered and said: "Tell that fox: Today and tomorrow I perform signs, and on the third day I am perfected." "Tell that fox"—that is, that crafty soul, full of deceit and of all wickedness and villainy. Have you understood, brother, how Scripture calls the cunning foxes? So when you say with the psalmist, "They shall go down into the depths of the earth; they shall be the portion of foxes," understand the riddle, and do not suppose that the riddle is to be taken except in a spiritual sense. And elsewhere again he said: "They shall be the portion of hypocrites." For those who do not know the truth take their portion not with the faithful but with the hypocrites. Hence the Saviour too, setting his seal on this meaning, says of the man who managed badly: "The master of that servant will come and cut him in two, and assign him his portion with the hypocrites." So Scripture called the hypocrites foxes. Into so many unseemly forms and likenesses, brothers, was the image of God brought down, that before the knowledge of godliness shone upon it, Scripture calls the whole world nothing other than irrational animals and cattle and reptiles and wild beasts. Indeed, when God, the lover of mankind, wished to persuade Peter, the chief of the apostles, to receive all who came over from the Gentiles, he showed him that wonderful and strange sheet let down from heaven by its four corners, in which were all the four-footed creatures of the earth, and the birds of the air, and the wild beasts and the reptiles; and he said to him: "Get up, Peter, kill and eat." But the apostle said: "By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean." For Peter, not understanding the riddle of the image and thinking that what he saw was physical, refused to eat, keeping the Jewish custom, and said: "By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean." But the Lord said to him: "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." These things, then, the Saviour said to the apostle about the four-footed creatures, the wild beasts and the birds that appeared to him. But Peter, the apostle of Christ, understood afterward that by the sheet the Saviour was hinting not at birds and wild beasts but at all the nations, and so he says to Cornelius in conversation with him: "You know that it is unlawful for a Jewish man to associate with a foreigner; but God has shown me that I should call no man common or unclean."

Have you learned, brother, how variously we have been disgraced by the names of irrational beasts? So when you read again in the prophet Isaiah, "Then the wolf shall graze with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the lion and the ox shall graze together and eat straw together," understand the riddle and grasp its meaning clearly: it does not announce a gathering of irrational wild beasts, but the fellowship of human beings. It plainly signifies the fellowship of godliness and the salvation that has shone forth through grace upon all people. For when you see in church a poor man standing beside a rich man, a commoner beside a ruler, a lowly man beside his superior, the one who outside trembles at his power, understand what is meant by "the wolf shall graze with the lamb." He calls the rich man a wolf, and the poor man a lamb. And why so? Because the wolf will share with the lamb, in the same way as the rich man with the poor. And pay close attention: often a rich man and a poor man are standing in church; the hour of the mysteries arrives; the rich man is sent out as uninitiated, while the poor man stands within the heavenly tabernacles. And the rich man is not indignant, for he knows that he is a stranger to the divine mysteries. O the divine grace! Not only is there equality of honour in the church through the grace of God, but even as they stand there, the poor man often takes precedence over the rich in godliness. His wealth has done its owner no good where godliness is concerned, nor has poverty harmed the believer; rather, it sets him with confidence before the holy altar.

I say these things, beloved, about the catechumens, and not about the rich in general. Consider, brother, how often a master withdraws from the church while a faithful servant remains for the mysteries; the mistress departs and the maidservant stays. "For God shows no partiality." So in the church there is no slave and free; rather, Scripture regards as a slave the one enslaved to sin. "For whoever commits sin," it says, "is a slave of sin." And it regards as free the one who has been set free by divine grace. "For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus," it says, "has set me free from the law of sin." Since, then, the image, as we said before, had been ruinously corrupted and broken down, the Saviour came and raised up his own image again. That which the devil had pulled down, the Creator put on, the lover of mankind becoming man—not disgracing his dignity, but displaying his love for humankind. This is why the blessed David, foretelling this divine and strange garment, said: "The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with majesty." The garment is not given to the Godhead, which is without beginning and without body—for nothing is more majestic than God, that God should need to clothe himself with majesty—but to human nature. For we human beings cover the unseemly parts of our bodies with the seemliness of our clothing. But God, who is simple and without shape, "who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light," what majesty does he need, or what garment does he put on? Clearly the prophet called the assumption of the body "majesty." He calls his own flesh "majesty," not because of the nature of the body, but because of its accomplishment in the virtues. That is why the Lord's body is majestic: not merely because it was a body, but because "he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." "The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with majesty." So too Isaiah says: "He will clothe all people and put them on like a bride's ornament." "The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself"; and: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one," and what follows. These words show Christ the King like a soldier, putting on, as it were, the armour of an earthly body. And rightly "earthly," for he does not arm himself in the way people do. Listen how. When we human beings arm ourselves, as we often do, we protect what is weak with what is strong. But God, being strong and mighty and powerful, puts on the earthly and weak body, not disgracing his dignity, but displaying through what is weak the surpassing greatness of his power, as he said when Paul entreated him: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Hence this noble apostle too, understanding well what had been said to him, says somewhere in writing to the Corinthians that "the weakness of God is stronger than men." "The Lord has clothed himself with strength"—that is, with the dispensation that shone forth through the flesh. For what is more powerful than that precious and holy flesh? What is stronger? For through a body he defeated the bodiless and wicked demons, and through the cross he triumphed over the opposing powers. Pay close attention. To be girded means to be circumscribed. Since, then, the holy and uncircumscribed nature seemed to be circumscribed in the body—not being circumscribed in its own nature, but thought to be circumscribed according to what was visible to the eye—he rightly said: "The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself." And what follows? "For he has established the world, which shall not be moved." Since sin had at first shaken the world, the Saviour came, planted the cross, and established the world. "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." And Paul says: "Nevertheless the firm foundation stands, bearing this seal." So the Master uttered two sayings: "On this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." He did not use a long string of words. He did not say: "I am establishing the church, and neither kings, nor rulers, nor tyrants, nor executioners, nor the wise, nor peasants, nor orators shall overcome the church"—for the kingdom of Christ is invincible and unconquerable. Rather, he indicated his power by a word and secured his promise with a bare phrase: "On this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." Two sayings—not bare sayings, but sayings of God. For he who established the heavens by a word and founded the earth by a word also built the church, walled it about, and "established the world, which shall not be moved."

Let us then fall down, beloved, before him who established the world, and weep, and implore him, so that through his love for mankind and his unspeakable power we may remain steadfast and immovable on the unshakable and unbreakable foundation, and may always offer up glory and thanksgiving to him, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
